Estimates, standard errors and site labels

Source: vignettes/data-input.Rmd
data-input.Rmd

This vignette shows how to pass estimates and standard errors to bayes_efron_fit() from a data frame, from metafor or as two vectors. It also shows where the site labels appear in the results, and how to compare a fit with the normal random-effects model from metafor.

library(bayesEfron)

The model needs two numbers for each site: an estimate of the effect and the standard error of that estimate. Data rarely arrive in that form. A table may have variances where standard errors are wanted, or the estimates may still have to be computed from the means, standard deviations and sample sizes of two groups. The sites (studies, firms, schools) usually have names as well, which you will want to see again beside the results. as_bef_data() handles the first case and, together with metafor::escalc(), the second, and a fit keeps the names.

Estimates in a data frame

We start with the callback data from vignette("bayesEfron"), which have one row for each of 97 firms.

head(krw_discrimination[, c("firm_name", "yi", "vi", "sei")], 4)
#>           firm_name          yi           vi        sei
#> 1          Rite Aid 0.046957123 0.0002622320 0.01619358
#> 2               KFC 0.022000000 0.0002342345 0.01530472
#> 3 Victoria's Secret 0.042161613 0.0005271759 0.02296031
#> 4    United Rentals 0.005708306 0.0002264274 0.01504751

yi is the difference between the callback probabilities of applications with distinctively white and distinctively Black names at the firm, vi its sampling variance and sei its standard error. The function as_bef_data() finds the two columns that it needs by their names, and its site argument names the column that contains the labels:

dat <- as_bef_data(krw_discrimination, site = "firm_name")
dat
#> <bef_data>
#> Sites: 97
#> Source: data.frame
#> theta_hat: min -0.02254; median 0.01781; max 0.09817
#> sigma: min 0.005344; median 0.01581; max 0.0392
#> Names: Rite Aid, KFC, Victoria's Secret, ...

It takes the first of these names that the data frame has, here yi and sei:

  • estimates: theta_hat, yi, estimate, effect, y;
  • standard errors: sigma, se, std_error, stderr, sei.

If your columns have other names, give them in the arguments theta_hat and sigma. If the second column contains variances, as vi does, set variance = TRUE and the function takes the square roots.

from_variances <- as_bef_data(krw_discrimination, sigma = "vi",
                              variance = TRUE, site = "firm_name")
all.equal(from_variances$sigma, dat$sigma)
#> [1] TRUE

as_bef_data() warns when a column with a name that begins with vi or var is given as the standard errors without variance = TRUE. It cannot detect variances under another name, because both are positive numbers, so check the range of sigma in the printed object.

The function throws an error if a value is missing, if a standard error is not positive, if a label occurs twice or if there are fewer than 5 sites. It does not drop incomplete rows, because the number of sites would then change without notice. For example, a missing standard error gives this error:

incomplete <- krw_discrimination
incomplete$sei[3] <- NA
try(as_bef_data(incomplete))
#> Error in as_bef_data(incomplete) : 
#>   Columns `yi` and `sei` must not contain missing values (found 0 and 1).

We can pass dat to bayes_efron_fit() as it is.

fit <- bayes_efron_fit(dat, seed = 20250807)

You can also pass the data frame itself when its columns have the names listed above. Its row names, if they have been set, are then the labels.

Group summaries and metafor

Often the estimates have not been computed yet, and each study reports the mean, the standard deviation and the size of two groups. From such summaries, metafor::escalc() computes an estimate and its sampling variance (Viechtbauer 2010), and as_bef_data() accepts its result.

As an example we apply escalc() to the 9 studies that Normand (1999) analyzed, which compare the length of hospital stay of stroke patients under specialized and under routine care. The data are in the metadat package, which metafor loads.

library(metafor)
stroke <- escalc(
  measure = "MD",
  m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
  m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i,
  data = dat.normand1999, slab = source
)
stroke[, c("source", "m1i", "m2i", "yi", "vi")]
#> 
#>               source m1i m2i       yi       vi 
#> 1          Edinburgh  55  75 -20.0000  40.5080 
#> 2     Orpington-Mild  27  29  -2.0000   2.0806 
#> 3 Orpington-Moderate  64 119 -55.0000  15.6984 
#> 4   Orpington-Severe  66 137 -71.0000 150.2222 
#> 5      Montreal-Home  14  18  -4.0000  17.3077 
#> 6  Montreal-Transfer  19  18   1.0000   1.1673 
#> 7          Newcastle  52  41  11.0000  94.5891 
#> 8               Umea  21  31 -10.0000   6.3109 
#> 9            Uppsala  30  23   7.0000  19.8423

We set measure = "MD", so the estimate yi is the difference between the two means, here in days, and vi is the sum of the two squared standard errors of the means, \(s_1^2 / n_1 + s_2^2 / n_2\). A difference in the original units is the natural choice when every study measures the outcome in the same way, as these do. When the studies use different instruments, as the teacher expectancy studies in vignette("teacher-expectancy") did with their IQ tests, the standardized mean difference (measure = "SMD") puts the estimates on a common scale.

From an escalc object, as_bef_data() takes the column yi as the estimates and the square roots of vi as the standard errors.

stroke_dat <- as_bef_data(stroke)
as.data.frame(stroke_dat)
#>   site              label estimate        se
#> 1    1          Edinburgh      -20  6.364591
#> 2    2     Orpington-Mild       -2  1.442444
#> 3    3 Orpington-Moderate      -55  3.962121
#> 4    4   Orpington-Severe      -71 12.256518
#> 5    5      Montreal-Home       -4  4.160251
#> 6    6  Montreal-Transfer        1  1.080436
#> 7    7          Newcastle       11  9.725694
#> 8    8               Umea      -10  2.512146
#> 9    9            Uppsala        7  4.454471

The labels are the ones given to escalc() in its slab argument. Without slab, row names that have been set are used.

Although 9 studies are enough for the function to run, we can learn little from them about the shape of the distribution of effects. With so few sites, the result depends strongly on the range of the grid, as vignette("teacher-expectancy") shows for 19 studies.

Two vectors

If your estimates and standard errors are two vectors, pass them to bayes_efron_fit() as its first two arguments. The names of the estimates, if they have any, become the labels. To have the two vectors checked before running a fit, give them to as_bef_data() as a list, in which an element names can supply the labels:

as_bef_data(list(
  theta_hat = krw_discrimination$yi,
  sigma = krw_discrimination$sei,
  names = krw_discrimination$firm_name
))
#> <bef_data>
#> Sites: 97
#> Source: list
#> theta_hat: min -0.02254; median 0.01781; max 0.09817
#> sigma: min 0.005344; median 0.01581; max 0.0392
#> Names: Rite Aid, KFC, Victoria's Secret, ...

Whatever the form, the estimates should be the original ones. Estimates that have already been shrunk, such as the posterior means from another model, are not independent noisy observations of the effects, and passing them as if they were changes the model.

Site labels in the results

A fit stores the site labels. To show this we use krw_fit, the fit of the callback data that comes with the package, made with the bayes_efron_fit() call above and thin = 15. Its table of site effects has the labels in the column label.

fit <- krw_fit
head(site_summary(fit)[, c("site", "label", "estimate", "mean", "lower",
                           "upper")], 4)
#>   site             label    estimate       mean        lower      upper
#> 1    1          Rite Aid 0.046957123 0.03048175  0.010775168 0.05349968
#> 2    2               KFC 0.022000000 0.01786494  0.001227187 0.03581179
#> 3    3 Victoria's Secret 0.042161613 0.02334782  0.002864899 0.04801767
#> 4    4    United Rentals 0.005708306 0.01071991 -0.005107269 0.02719213

You can choose a site by its label wherever a function takes sites, and the returned vectors are named by label. Here we pick four firms and print, for each, the probability of a positive gap and the posterior mean in percentage points:

chosen <- c("Rite Aid", "KFC", "Safeway", "Genuine Parts (Napa Auto)")
round(exceedance_prob(fit, sites = chosen), 3)
#>                  Rite Aid                       KFC                   Safeway 
#>                     0.997                     0.962                     0.835 
#> Genuine Parts (Napa Auto) 
#>                     1.000
round(100 * coef(fit)[chosen], 2)
#>                  Rite Aid                       KFC                   Safeway 
#>                      3.05                      1.79                      1.14 
#> Genuine Parts (Napa Auto) 
#>                      6.41

The plots show the labels as well, here for the same four firms.

plot_sites(fit, sites = chosen, scale = 100)

Without labels a site is identified by its number, which is its position in the input, so keep the rows of your data in the order in which they were fitted. If the sites have labels, that order no longer matters for finding a site.

Comparison with the normal model from metafor

A metafor user will want to see the result next to the normal random-effects model. We plot the estimated distribution of effects with plot_g(), and normal = TRUE adds that model: a normal distribution with its mean and standard deviation estimated from the same estimates by restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

plot_g(fit, normal = TRUE, scale = 100)

The dashed curve leaves out the uncertainty of its two parameters, whereas the band around the solid curve is a posterior interval. See vignette("bayesEfron") for what we can conclude about the callback gaps from the two curves.

The same two numbers come from metafor::rma() once its iteration is allowed to run to convergence, here with a smaller threshold:

loose <- rma(yi, vi, data = krw_discrimination, method = "REML")
tight <- rma(yi, vi, data = krw_discrimination, method = "REML",
             control = list(threshold = 1e-10))
rbind(default = c(mean = coef(loose)[[1]], sd = sqrt(loose$tau2)),
      tightened = c(mean = coef(tight)[[1]], sd = sqrt(tight$tau2)))
#>                 mean         sd
#> default   0.01655591 0.01464373
#> tightened 0.01654070 0.01458854

By default rma() stops when its estimate of the variance of the effects changes by less than \(10^{-5}\) from one step to the next. That is early for estimates on a small scale. The variance of these gaps is about 0.0002, and the default leaves the standard deviation 0.4% away from the value at convergence, which is the value that plot_g() shows. To plot a normal model fitted in another way, give its two numbers as normal = c(mean = ..., sd = ...).

References

Normand, Sharon-Lise T. 1999. “Meta-Analysis: Formulating, Evaluating, Combining, and Reporting.” Statistics in Medicine 18 (3): 321–59. https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19990215)18:3<321::AID-SIM28>3.0.CO;2-P.
Viechtbauer, Wolfgang. 2010. “Conducting Meta-Analyses in R with the metafor Package.” Journal of Statistical Software 36 (3). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v036.i03.
